newsitem.title: USA: Russia reneges on missile defenses deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia reneges on missile defenses deal.

text.p: Russia at the last moment has backed away from an agreement on regional missile defences that was set for signing on Oct. 31, U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

"This has been called off. There'll be no signing ceremony in Geneva on Thursday ... We're disappointed by Russia's reversal of its own position," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Another official told Reuters: "We had a set of documents that was agreed by all sides. Texts were confirmed. Translators had certified the documents meant the same thing. We had a time and place for the signing and people were flying in from all (relevant) capitals. We were all set."

The collapse of the deal Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov reaffirmed in New York on Sept. 23 is a blow to Clinton administration arms control efforts.
It also raises new questions about how the power struggle in Moscow is affecting Russian policy and the ability of the United States and Russia to deal cooperatively.

Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, in the toughest U.S. assessment of Russia recently, warned Moscow in a speech on Tuesday against perpetuating worst-case Cold War fears about the United States, saying it could undermine cooperation.
At Wednesday's news briefing, Burns stressed: "Russia needs to make sure it does not isolate itself in the future."
The agreement announced by Christopher and Primakov last month would specify which short-range defence missile systems are allowed under the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty.

Deploying regional defences against missiles has become increasingly popular in recent years -- especially among Republicans -- as the United States confronted dangers posed by missiles controlled by renegade states, like Iran and Iraq.

But the prospect of theatre missile defences has also raised concerns about undermining the ABM treaty, which was designed to limit strategic defences so they do not overwhelm the nuclear weapons agreements that have helped keep a power balance -- and peace -- between the United States and Russia.

The ABM pact, considered by many experts a cornerstone of international arms control, limits defences against strategic -- or long-range -- missiles but was not meant to address regional -- or "theater" -- missile defences.
But the United States and Russia had been negotiating what systems could be pursued legally under the treaty.

At their September meeting in New York, Christopher and Primakov agreed to permit deployment of lower-speed theatre missile defence systems of up to two miles (3 km) per second provided they are not tested against faster, longer-range ballistic missile targets.
Russia had been wavering on whether to delay signing this accord until a more controversial second-phase pact governing faster systems was also agreed.
But Primakov's September announcement with Christopher, and subsequent Russian commitments, gave confidence the first-phase deal would go forward on Oct 31.

Then late last week, Russia signalled the two accords would have to be joined, a linkage U.S. officials said they could not accept. They worked feverishly on Tuesday to see if the deal could be saved but failed.

Burns refused to speculate on what internal Russian dynamics caused the reversal but clearly put the onus on Primakov. "The Russian foreign minister made a very specific agreement with Secretary of State Christopher. We expect that should be honoured," he said.
One U.S. official said progress has been made on the second-phase agreement "but it's not about to be signed."

Officials said they would continue to discuss missile defences with Moscow and hoped to eventually reach agreement. Besides this problem, Russia's parliament is holding up the START 2 nuclear arms reduction treaty and the U.S. Senate has delayed ratifying the Chemical Weapons Convention.
